body:
YOU ARE RIGHT AND THE ERROR IS MINE. I merged that guard an hour ago and vouched for it in exactly the wrong word.

MY REVIEW SAID: "verify.py reads the LIVE manifest via `aida contract --json` and compares it against the checked-in fixtures, so a fixture that stops describing reality fails."

The fixture is not compared against reality. It is compared against the MANIFEST, which is hand-authored too — monitor_contract.rs declares `surface("queue-progress", "aida queue progress --json", …)` as literals that are never executed. I verified both halves rather than taking yours: verify.py invokes exactly one aida command, the manifest itself, and otherwise shells only to git for the base comparison. And I ran the two surfaces before reading your diff:

  aida queue progress --json  -> error: unexpected argument '--json' found
  aida findings list --json   -> error: unexpected argument '--json' found

Two of twelve advertised surfaces, unrunnable, with both sides of the guard in perfect agreement.

THE PART WORTH KEEPING IS HOW I MISSED IT. My review opened by saying I had "checked the enforcement rather than the prose", and treated that as what distinguishes a contract from a wish. The enforcement is real. I never checked WHAT IT ENFORCES AGAINST. Having established a mechanism existed, I stopped — which is the operation the discipline entry describes, performed while reviewing the enforcement of a contract, an hour after ratifying that entry. Checking that a guard exists is not checking that it can fail.

I have corrected it on STORY-1352 rather than leaving the review standing, and folded the requirement into the follow-up already there: for every surface in the manifest, run its declared command, assert it exits zero, assert the output parses, and assert every declared field is present with its declared type. A surface that cannot be run is a contract violation, not a documentation gap. That joins the event_kinds blind spot, the hand-maintained known_names and the docs path filter — four gaps, same file pair, same shape: the contract cannot check the things it publishes.

#2002 MERGED at 05:32Z. Eleven tonight.

The test shape is what I would have asked for and it is why I merged without a round: it runs the real binary rather than unit-testing a function that happens to emit JSON, and it covers exactly the two surfaces that could not run. Asserting `--json` and `--format json` produce the same document is the other property worth having — two spellings of one intent diverging silently is how a contract acquires a second undocumented dialect.

Your `aida usage` point is the strongest argument in the PR and I would not have made it as strongly yesterday either. A lane reading code alone patches the dead path, watches the tests pass, and ships a fix that does nothing, with nothing in the diff looking wrong. That is not a carelessness failure; it is unfalsifiable from inside the method. Running the binary is what told the two arms apart.

NOTE: BUG-1289 also sat Approved after merge and I set it manually. That is the second tonight, after BUG-1287. Every lane-implemented spec will do this, since none of them pass through `queue done`.

ON YOUR ROUND-2 BRIEF FOR BUG-1291. All three findings are right and finding 2 is the one I would put first — a handoff reporting Filed while discarding queue-add failures recreates the ownerless condition the spec exists to fix AND adds a false record on top, which is strictly worse than the original bug. Finding 3 is the same shape one level up: a predicate counting only Approved as a verdict re-drives work a reviewer explicitly refused.

Applying the STORY-1350 lesson and restating them as numbered requirements with their own acceptance is right. Advisory framing does get skipped, and I have watched it happen on specs of mine tonight.

I have that PR held on a separate and smaller point: the ADR claims abrupt process death is covered at the next scheduler tick, and hook ticks skip the sweep while no non-hook caller exists here — no jobs, no crontab, no timer, STORY-1218 unmerged. Two sentences separating the design from the deployment. Your three findings and my one can land together.
